title: Squeezing Enhancement In Lossy Multi-Path Atom Interferometers
authors: Julian Günther, Jan-Niclas Kirsten-Siemß, Naceur Gaaloul, And Klemens Hammerer
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2122 (2026).

This paper explores the sensitivity gains afforded by spin-squeezed states in atom interferometry, in particular using Bragg diffraction. We introduce a generalised input-output formalism that accurately describes realistic, non-unitary interferometers, including losses due to velocity selectivity and scattering into undesired momentum states. This formalism is applied to evaluate the performance of one-axis twisted spin-squeezed states in improving phase sensitivity. Our results show that by carefully optimising the parameters of the Bragg beam splitters and controlling the degree of squeezing, it is possible to improve the sensitivity of the interferometer by several dB with respect to the standard quantum limit despite realistic levels of losses in light pulse operations. However, the analysis also highlights the challenges associated with achieving these improvements in practice, most notably the impact of finite temperature on the benefits of entanglement. The results suggest ways of optimising interferometric setups to exploit quantum entanglement under realistic conditions, thereby contributing to advances in precision metrology with atom interferometers.

.
tldr: This paper analyzes sensitivity gains from spin-squeezed states in lossy multi-path atom interferometers using a generalized input-output formalism.
motivation: To understand how spin-squeezed states can improve phase sensitivity in realistic atom interferometers with losses, and to optimize parameters for practical quantum-enhanced metrology.
method: Developed a generalized input-output formalism for non-unitary interferometers including losses from velocity selectivity and scattering, and applied it to evaluate one-axis twisted spin-squeezed states.
result: Optimizing Bragg beam splitter parameters and squeezing degree can yield several dB improvement over the standard quantum limit despite losses, but finite temperature reduces the benefits of entanglement.
conclusion: The results provide guidelines for designing interferometers that exploit quantum entanglement under realistic conditions, advancing precision metrology with atom interferometers.

title: On The Dynamical Lie Algebras Of Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithms
authors: Jonathan Allcock, Miklos Santha, Pei Yuan, And Shengyu Zhang
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2119 (2026).

Dynamical Lie algebras (DLAs) have emerged as a valuable tool in the study of parameterized quantum circuits, helping to characterize both their expressiveness and trainability. In particular, the absence or presence of barren plateaus (BPs) – flat regions in parameter space that prevent the efficient training of variational quantum algorithms – has recently been shown to be intimately related to quantities derived from the associated DLA. In this work, we investigate DLAs for the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA), one of the most studied variational quantum algorithms for solving graph MaxCut and other combinatorial optimization problems. While DLAs for QAOA circuits have been studied before, existing results have either been based on numerical evidence, or else correspond to DLA generators specifically chosen to be universal for quantum computation on a subspace of states. We initiate an analytical study of barren plateaus and other statistics of QAOA algorithms, and give bounds on the dimensions of the corresponding DLAs and their centers for general graphs. We then focus on the [MATH]-vertex cycle and complete graphs. For the cycle graph we give an explicit basis, identify its decomposition into the direct sum of a [MATH]-dimensional center and a semisimple component isomorphic to [MATH] copies of [MATH]. We give an explicit basis for this isomorphism, and a closed-form expression for the variance of the cost function, proving the absence of BPs. For the complete graph we prove that the dimension of the DLA is [MATH] and give an explicit basis for the DLA.

.
tldr: This paper analytically studies dynamical Lie algebras of QAOA circuits for cycle and complete graphs, proving absence of barren plateaus for cycle graphs and giving explicit DLA dimensions and bases.
motivation: To understand the trainability and expressiveness of QAOA, particularly the presence of barren plateaus, which hinder variational quantum algorithms.
method: Analytical derivation of DLA dimensions, centers, and decompositions for general graphs, with explicit calculations for cycle and complete graphs using representation theory.
result: For cycle graphs, the DLA decomposes into a 1D center and a semisimple component isomorphic to copies of su(2), leading to a closed-form variance of the cost function and proving no barren plateaus. For complete graphs, the DLA dimension is n^2 - 1 with an explicit basis.
conclusion: The work provides rigorous analytical results on QAOA DLAs, enabling better understanding of trainability, but the specific graphs studied are limited and may not generalize to more complex problems.

title: Reply To "Interpreting Bohm Quantum Potentials In `Computing Quantum Waves Exactly From Classical Action'"
authors: Gabor Vattay
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05197v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The recent arXiv posting arXiv:2605.20443 by Lohmiller and Slotine attempts to address the omission of the Bohm quantum potential in their proposed exact equivalence between classical action and the Schr\"odinger equation. They introduce a position-dependent time transformation to argue that the spatial derivatives of the probability density amplitude vanish for the Feynman kernel. A rigorous mathematical examination of this transformation reveals a violation of the multivariable chain rule. The spatial derivatives do not vanish in the physical reference frame. The mathematical framework presented by the authors remains identical to the well-established semiclassical Van Vleck propagator, which is exact exclusively for quadratic potentials.
tldr: This reply refutes a claim that the Schrödinger equation can be exactly derived from classical action by showing that the proposed position-dependent time transformation violates the multivariable chain rule, and that the resulting propagator is merely the semiclassical Van Vleck propagator.
motivation: To correct a mathematical error in a previous arXiv posting that claimed an exact equivalence between classical action and the Schrödinger equation via a position-dependent time transformation.
method: Rigorous mathematical examination of the transformation, checking the multivariable chain rule and comparing the resulting propagator to known semiclassical results.
result: The transformation violates the chain rule, and the spatial derivatives of the probability density amplitude do not vanish in the physical frame; the framework reduces to the semiclassical Van Vleck propagator, which is exact only for quadratic potentials.
conclusion: The claimed exact equivalence is invalid; the Bohm quantum potential is essential for exact quantum dynamics, and the semiclassical approximation remains limited to quadratic potentials.

title: xCPS: An xAct Package For Covariant Phase Space, Noether Charges, And Entropy
authors: Juan Margalef-Bentabol
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05204v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: xCPS is an xAct tensor algebra package for symbolic computations within the covariant phase space formalism of field theories. From a generic Lagrangian, xCPS automates the derivation of equations of motion and symplectic currents. It systematically determines whether an infinitesimal transformation in the space of fields is a Noether symmetry and computes the associated Noether charge. Additionally, xCPS can in many cases determine whether a tensorial expression is a divergence and, if so, find its divergence potential. By implementing vertical exterior calculus through a graded, supercommutative wedge product and vertical operators, the package enables efficient computations in gauge theories and higher-derivative models of gravity, including the derivation of thermodynamic quantities like Wald's entropy. xCPS is open-source under the GPL license and available at [URL].
tldr: xCPS is a tensor algebra package for symbolic computations in covariant phase space formalism, automating derivation of equations of motion, Noether charges, and Wald entropy.
motivation: To provide a computational tool for researchers working on covariant phase space methods, especially in gauge theories and higher-derivative gravity, where manual calculations are error-prone and time-consuming.
method: The package implements vertical exterior calculus with graded supercommutative wedge products and vertical operators within the xAct tensor algebra framework for Mathematica.
result: xCPS can derive equations of motion, symplectic currents, Noether symmetries and charges, and divergence potentials from a generic Lagrangian, and compute thermodynamic quantities like Wald entropy.
conclusion: The package facilitates efficient symbolic computations in covariant phase space, enabling further research in gravitational thermodynamics and gauge theories, but its direct relevance to the user's interests is limited.

title: Isospectrality And Operator Complexity
authors: Pradip Kattel, Yicheng Tang, Natan Andrei
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05294v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study a pair of exactly solvable, isospectral fermion chains, one strongly interacting and one quadratic, that nevertheless display remarkably different phase structures and operator dynamics. A nonlocal nonlinear unitary transformation maps one onto the other while preserving the entire many-body spectrum and converting local fermion operators into extended many-body strings. Thus, operators that evolve within a closed linear subspace in the quadratic model become interacting operators that generate increasingly higher-body terms and exhibit asymptotic Lanczos growth [MATH]. Despite their identical spectra, the two models realize distinct phases and sharply different notions of operator complexity. Our results demonstrate that free many-body spectra and interacting operator dynamics are fundamentally compatible.
tldr: Two isospectral fermion chains, one interacting and one quadratic, exhibit identical spectra but vastly different operator complexity and phase structures.
motivation: To understand how operator complexity can differ despite spectral equivalence, challenging the notion that free spectra imply simple dynamics.
method: Constructed a nonlocal nonlinear unitary transformation mapping a quadratic fermion chain to a strongly interacting one, preserving the spectrum but converting local operators into many-body strings.
result: The quadratic model shows linear Lanczos growth, while the interacting model exhibits asymptotic growth, indicating higher operator complexity; the two models realize distinct phases.
conclusion: Free many-body spectra are compatible with interacting operator dynamics, highlighting that spectral information alone does not determine dynamical complexity.

title: Setting Angles In Quantum Approximate Optimization At Utility-scale
authors: Maosheng Guo, Joel Jurado Diaz, Anurag Ramesh, Conrad J. Haupt, Alberto Baiardi, Dimitrios Athanasakos, M. Emre Sahin, Oscar Wallis, George Pennington, Christian Arenz, Sebastian Brandhofer, Georgios Korpas, Ieva \v{c}epait\.e, J. A. Monta\~nez-Barrera, Jakub Marecek, Davide Venturelli, Stephan Eidenbenz, David E. Bernal Neira, Daniel J. Egger
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05311v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) is a powerful heuristic that seeks to solve combinatorial optimization problems using quantum hardware and classical optimization in tandem. Various methods exist to train the parameterized quantum circuits that serve as an ansatz in QAOA. However, which method works best to identify optimal angles for a given problem instance remains poorly understood, especially at utility-scale, i.e., [MATH] qubits or more. In this work, we address this challenge through utility-scale benchmarks from which we distill operational guidance for QAOA practitioners. First, we investigate approximation techniques, such as matrix product states and Pauli propagation, to find optimal angles. Second, we train QAOA on small-scale representative problems and transfer the angles to larger ones. We then validate the results on quantum hardware for utility-scale problem instances that can be meaningfully executed. In this way, we identify insights for QAOA angle setting strategies that work best for problems at the utility scale, including as a function of resource cost for the search. Crucially, the operational implications we draw from our benchmarks will help quantum optimization practitioners execute QAOA end-to-end pipelines efficiently on current and future hardware.
tldr: This paper benchmarks angle-setting strategies for QAOA at utility-scale (≥100 qubits) using classical approximations and angle transfer, validated on quantum hardware.
motivation: To determine which methods for training QAOA parameters work best for large problem instances, as current understanding is limited at utility-scale.
method: Benchmarked matrix product states and Pauli propagation for angle optimization, and transferred angles from small to large instances; validated on quantum hardware.
result: Identified effective angle-setting strategies and their resource costs for utility-scale QAOA, providing operational guidance.
conclusion: The findings help practitioners efficiently execute QAOA on current and future quantum hardware, but the paper focuses on combinatorial optimization rather than the user's research interests.

title: Multi-Qubit Dyadic Phase Fixing For Fault-Tolerant Quantum Compilation
authors: Justin Kalloor, Mathias Weiden, Ed Younis, John Kubiatowicz, Costin Iancu
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05397v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires translating application-level quantum circuits into the Clifford+[MATH] gate set, where the [MATH] gate is the dominant resource cost. Phase kickback is an ancilla-based technique that can dramatically reduce [MATH]-count for rotations with dyadic angles, but has previously been limited to highly structured circuit families. We present Dyadic Phase Fixing (DPF), a general multi-qubit synthesis tool that extends phase kickback to general quantum circuits. DPF uses numerical unitary synthesis to greedily extract dyadic angle rotations from any input circuit. Combined with a decision matrix to automatically size the final phase gradient register, our end-to-end workflow achieves up to 70% reduction in [MATH]-count compared to and up to 60% compared to Repeat-Until-Success synthesis on a diverse set of benchmarks. We map these compiled circuits to a surface-code architecture to evaluate space-time volume, demonstrating up to a 60\% reduction in this metric as well. However, for some circuits and mapping strategies the two metrics diverge significantly, demonstrating that [MATH]-count alone is a useful but incomplete proxy for fault-tolerant program costs.
tldr: This paper presents a method to reduce T-gate count in fault-tolerant quantum circuits by extending phase kickback to general circuits via numerical unitary synthesis.
motivation: T-gates are expensive in fault-tolerant quantum computing, and existing phase kickback techniques are limited to structured circuits. The authors aim to generalize this approach to arbitrary circuits.
method: They propose Dyadic Phase Fixing (DPF), which uses numerical unitary synthesis to greedily extract dyadic angle rotations from any circuit, combined with a decision matrix to size the phase gradient register.
result: DPF achieves up to 70% reduction in T-count and up to 60% reduction in space-time volume on diverse benchmarks compared to prior methods.
conclusion: T-count reduction is a useful but incomplete proxy for fault-tolerant costs; the method significantly improves compilation efficiency for fault-tolerant quantum computing.

title: Newton's Identity In Finite-Bead Fermionic Partition Function
authors: J. Valenzuela A. Chaudhary
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05442v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For non-interacting fermions in a harmonic trap, the partition function at any discrete number of imaginary time slices (or beads) and for any choice of short-time propagator admits an exact recursion relation derived directly from the contracted determinant form of the path integral. This finite-bead recursion is distinct from earlier continuum-limit recursions, which do not apply to the discrete time partition functions. By identifying a direct correspondence between this recursion and Newton's identity, application of a closed-form result from the theory of partitions provides an exact expression for the one-dimensional [MATH]-fermion finite-bead partition function. From this, the Thermodynamic and Hamiltonian energies and specific heats are analytically calculated for any [MATH], [MATH], [MATH], and propagator choice.
tldr: This paper derives exact finite-bead partition functions for non-interacting fermions in a harmonic trap using Newton's identity.
motivation: To obtain exact expressions for the partition function at discrete imaginary time slices, which are not captured by continuum-limit recursions.
method: The authors derive a recursion relation from the contracted determinant form of the path integral and map it to Newton's identity, then apply a closed-form result from partition theory.
result: Exact one-dimensional N-fermion finite-bead partition function, from which thermodynamic and Hamiltonian energies and specific heats are analytically calculated for any N, bead number, temperature, and propagator choice.
conclusion: The work provides a complete analytic solution for finite-bead fermionic path integrals, enabling exact calculations without numerical extrapolation.

title: Decoder-Consistent Hamiltonians For POVM-Based Quantum Relaxations
authors: Takayuki Suzuki
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05604v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In compression-based quantum relaxations like QRAO, classical variables are encoded into qubits and decoded after optimization. We formalize that the choice of the quantum Hamiltonian is fundamentally determined by this decoder. By representing the decoder as a POVM, we define a unique decoder-consistent Hamiltonian via the pullback of the post-decoding expected objective value. Using this framework, we reveal that standard QRAO Hamiltonians are inconsistent for certain mixed-degree quadratic functions, and we provide new approximation guarantees for the MaxCut problem based directly on POVM decoder design.
tldr: This paper formalizes decoder-consistent Hamiltonians for POVM-based quantum relaxations, revealing inconsistencies in standard QRAO Hamiltonians and providing new approximation guarantees for MaxCut.
motivation: To address inconsistencies in quantum relaxation optimization (QRAO) where the choice of quantum Hamiltonian is not always aligned with the decoder, leading to suboptimal approximations.
method: The authors represent the decoder as a POVM and define a unique decoder-consistent Hamiltonian via pullback of the post-decoding expected objective value.
result: They show that standard QRAO Hamiltonians are inconsistent for certain mixed-degree quadratic functions and provide new approximation guarantees for MaxCut based on POVM decoder design.
conclusion: The framework enables better design of quantum relaxations by ensuring consistency between Hamiltonian and decoder, with implications for optimization problems like MaxCut.

title: Broadband Chromatic Dispersion Of Thermo-refractive Coefficients And Its Impact In Silicon Nitride Nonlinear Photonics
authors: Shao-Chien Ou, Gregory Moille, Kartik Srinivasan
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05673v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The thermo-refractive effect is a cornerstone of frequency and phase tuning in photonic integrated circuits. In particular, it enables control of phase-matching for integrated nonlinear processes. Chromatic dispersion of the group and effective refractive indices and modal confinement are standard considerations in design, but material thermo-refractive coefficients (TRCs) are typically taken to be fixed for the guiding and cladding materials. Here, we demonstrate that the assumption of non-dispersive TRCs across an octave of bandwidth between the telecom and visible results in a significant discrepancy between measured and simulated resonance frequencies of an integrated Si3N4/SiO2 microring resonator. We uncover a 7 % variation in Si3N4 and SiO2 material TRCs across this range, finding that the variation of dneff /dT from material TRCs is 1.3 times that from modal confinement. This accurately matches a temperature-dependent Lorentz oscillator model describing their chromatic dispersion. By integrating these dispersive TRCs into a multi-physics finite-element model, we achieve precise correspondence with experimentally measured temperature-dependent resonance frequency shifts across the octave, including in the context of second harmonic generation devices. Our results provide a physical framework and a universal predictive workflow for the design of high-efficiency, multi-wavelength nonlinear optical processes, fundamentally improving the thermal control of integrated photonic devices.
tldr: This paper investigates the chromatic dispersion of thermo-refractive coefficients in Si3N4/SiO2 microring resonators and its impact on nonlinear photonics, showing that dispersive TRCs are necessary for accurate modeling across an octave bandwidth.
motivation: Thermo-refractive coefficients are typically assumed non-dispersive, but this leads to discrepancies between measured and simulated resonance frequencies in integrated photonic devices, especially over broad bandwidths.
method: The authors used temperature-dependent Lorentz oscillator models and multi-physics finite-element simulations to capture the chromatic dispersion of TRCs, and validated against experimental measurements of resonance shifts in Si3N4/SiO2 microring resonators.
result: They found a 7% variation in Si3N4 and SiO2 TRCs across the telecom-to-visible octave, with the variation in dneff/dT from material TRCs being 1.3 times that from modal confinement.
conclusion: Incorporating dispersive TRCs improves thermal control and design of multi-wavelength nonlinear photonic devices, providing a predictive workflow for high-efficiency integrated photonics.

title: Towards Stable And Accurate Electron Dynamics Via Neural Network Based Time-dependent Variational Monte Carlo
authors: Weizhong Fu, Zhe Li, Yubing Qian, Ruichen Li, Weiluo Ren, Ji Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05850v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Real-time dynamics of interacting electrons lies at the interface between quantum mechanics and non-equilibrium physics, governing the microscopic origin of ultrafast phenomena of molecules and nano-materials. Though neural network variational Monte Carlo has achieved unprecedented accuracy for stationary state calculations, its extension to real-time evolution remains challenging. In this work, we introduce the neural basis time-dependent variational Monte Carlo framework, which achieves stable and highly accurate simulations of electron dynamics. By constraining the time evolution to a compact, customized manifold spanned by the neural basis, we effectively bypass instability issues and achieve long-term stable evolution. Moreover, we demonstrate that this framework yields benchmark-quality accuracy in simulating the laser-driven dipole responses of the hydrogen atom and a stretched hydrogen molecule, and accurately extracts the dynamic polarizabilities of helium and beryllium atoms. Our work reveals the vast potential of neural network wavefunctions for accurately describing real-time electron dynamics and establishes a promising new route for first-principles simulations of complex, time-dependent electronic phenomena.
tldr: This paper introduces a neural network-based time-dependent variational Monte Carlo method for stable and accurate simulation of electron dynamics.
motivation: Real-time dynamics of interacting electrons is crucial for understanding ultrafast phenomena, but extending neural network variational Monte Carlo to real-time evolution has been challenging due to instability issues.
method: The authors propose the neural basis time-dependent variational Monte Carlo framework, which constrains time evolution to a compact manifold spanned by a neural basis to bypass instability and achieve long-term stable evolution.
result: The method achieves benchmark-quality accuracy in simulating laser-driven dipole responses of hydrogen atom and stretched hydrogen molecule, and accurately extracts dynamic polarizabilities of helium and beryllium atoms.
conclusion: This work demonstrates the potential of neural network wavefunctions for real-time electron dynamics and opens a new route for first-principles simulations of time-dependent electronic phenomena.

title: Symmetry-adapted Qubit Encoding With Complete Active Space And Bravyi--Kitaev Mapping For Quantum Chemistry On A Quantum Computer
authors: Jonathan Tennyson Dario Picozzi
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05865v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a symmetry-adapted qubit encoding with complete active space (SAE-CAS) for quantum chemistry on fault-tolerant and near-term quantum processors. Building on exact-symmetry encodings, we extend symmetry-adapted mappings to approximate [MATH]-symmetries corresponding to frozen-core and virtual orbitals, thereby reducing qubit requirements without significant loss of accuracy. We derive the mapping from the second-quantised Hamiltonian to active-space qubit Hamiltonians, prove its equivalence to the canonical CAS Hamiltonian with frozen-core and virtual-orbital projection, and integrate it with point-group and spin-parity symmetry encodings via affine Clifford transformations to maximise qubit reduction while preserving the target symmetry sector. The same framework also accommodates the Bravyi--Kitaev mapping, yielding an SAE-CAS-BK variant that is unitarily equivalent to SAE-CAS. Numerical benchmarking on nine small molecules using UCCSD and a hardware-efficient shifted-circular-alternating (HE-SCA) ansatz shows that SAE-CAS reduces qubit counts and Pauli-operator weight, yields shallower circuits with fewer parameters, and often accelerates VQE convergence; with HE-SCA it consistently reaches CAS reference energies in cases where JW-CAS does not converge within the tested budgets. We provide an open-source implementation in the Python package QuantumSymmetry. SAE-CAS offers a route to resource-efficient molecular simulations on fault-tolerant and near-term quantum processors.
tldr: This paper presents a symmetry-adapted qubit encoding method for quantum chemistry that reduces qubit requirements by exploiting approximate symmetries, but it is not directly related to the user's research interests in information thermodynamics, quantum foundations, quantum communication, or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: Quantum chemistry simulations on quantum computers require many qubits; the authors aim to reduce qubit counts by encoding symmetries more efficiently.
method: They extend symmetry-adapted mappings to approximate symmetries (frozen-core and virtual orbitals), integrate point-group and spin-parity symmetries via affine Clifford transformations, and also incorporate the Bravyi–Kitaev mapping.
result: The SAE-CAS method reduces qubit counts and Pauli weight, yields shallower circuits, and often accelerates VQE convergence, achieving CAS reference energies with a hardware-efficient ansatz.
conclusion: The method offers a resource-efficient route for molecular simulations on near-term and fault-tolerant quantum processors, with an open-source implementation provided.

title: Single-Frequency Symmetry-Empowered Through-Barrier Sensing In Reconfigurable Complex Media
authors: Shuai S. A. Yuan, Viktar Asadchy, Philipp Del Hougne
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05877v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mirror symmetry can strongly enhance the transmission of waves through a barrier inside a complex medium. We recently showed that this phenomenon enables quantitative through-barrier sensing: by tuning programmable scatterers on one side of the barrier to maximize the broadband total transmission through the barrier, the characteristics of scatterers at mirror-symmetric positions on the other side of the barrier can be determined. Considering a sufficiently large bandwidth was crucial to ensure that no accidental narrowband asymmetric resonance can outperform the symmetry-induced transmission enhancement. Here, we overcome this scheme's vexing need for a large bandwidth by replacing the underlying frequency diversity with configurational diversity. Specifically, we introduce auxiliary tunable scatterers at mirror-symmetric positions on either side of the barrier and sweep their characteristics through a series of random mirror-symmetric configurations. We tune the programmable main scatterers on one side of the barrier to maximize the average of the total through-barrier transmission over a series of configurations of the auxiliary scatterers at a single frequency, in order to sense the characteristics of the main scatterers on the other side of the barrier. We systematically study the accuracy of our single-frequency sensing scheme based on a multiport-network system model that cascades two mirror-related wave-chaotic cavities with a weakly transmitting barrier in between. We further examine an extension to non-reciprocal chaotic cavities involving circulators. Altogether, our results establish configurational diversity as a route to single-frequency, symmetry-empowered through-barrier sensing in reconfigurable complex media.
tldr: This paper uses configurational diversity at a single frequency to perform through-barrier sensing in complex media, replacing the need for broadband measurements.
motivation: Previous symmetry-empowered through-barrier sensing required large bandwidth to avoid accidental asymmetric resonances; the authors aim to eliminate this bandwidth requirement.
method: The authors introduce auxiliary tunable scatterers at mirror-symmetric positions on both sides of the barrier and sweep their configurations randomly. They tune the main scatterers to maximize average transmission over these configurations at a single frequency, using a multiport-network model of two wave-chaotic cavities with a weak barrier.
result: The single-frequency scheme achieves accurate sensing of scatterer characteristics, and the method is extended to non-reciprocal cavities with circulators.
conclusion: Configurational diversity enables single-frequency symmetry-empowered through-barrier sensing, which may simplify experimental implementations and broaden applications in complex media.

title: A Comprehensive Survey On Semantic Communication In Non-Terrestrial Networks: Architectures, Methodologies, And Challenges
authors: Loc X. Nguyen, Avi Deb Raha, Huy Q. Le, Zhu Han, Eui-Nam Huh, Choong Seon Hong
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05216v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The sixth-generation wireless networks are envisioned to deliver ubiquitous, seamless, and intelligent connectivity that reaches far beyond the limits of terrestrial infrastructure. Non-terrestrial networks (NTNs) are central to this vision, extending coverage to underserved regions, remote terrain, and disaster zones that terrestrial deployment cannot economically reach. However, NTN architecture faces numerous limitations: severe path loss over long distances, long propagation delays, large and time-varying Doppler shifts, limited visibility windows, and tight on-board energy and computing budgets. Semantic communication (SemCom), which conveys the meaning of data rather than its raw bit-level representation, is unusually well matched to these conditions: extreme compression rate for task-oriented eases bandwidth scarcity, deep joint source-channel coding prevents the cliff effect due to low signal-to-noise ratio, and generative-AI reconstructs content from sparse cues that survive rain-faded or blocked links. This observation, that each NTN limitation maps onto a SemCom property that addresses it, motivates our survey. We first walk through the NTN limitations one by one, pairing each with the SemCom design choices that complement it, then we organize the literature along three axes: the NTN platform, the semantic methodology, and the supporting techniques, and follow this with platform-by-platform deep dives on satellite-centric, UAV/HAPS-centric, and integrated SAGIN systems. The survey concludes by identifying open research problems, gaps in existing standards, and future directions, including the application of foundation models, energy-aware scheduling, and quantum-assisted SemCom for deep space communication.
tldr: A survey on semantic communication in non-terrestrial networks, with a brief mention of quantum-assisted SemCom for deep space.
motivation: To address limitations of NTNs (path loss, delay, Doppler, energy) by leveraging semantic communication.
method: Literature survey organized by NTN platform, semantic methodology, and supporting techniques.
result: Identifies that each NTN limitation can be mitigated by a SemCom property; reviews satellite, UAV/HAPS, and SAGIN systems.
conclusion: Open problems include foundation models, energy-aware scheduling, and quantum-assisted SemCom for deep space.

title: Gradient Descent At The Edge Of Stability: Free Energy Model And Kinetic Description Of The Two-layer Network
authors: Antonin Chodron de Courcel
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05326v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the dynamics of gradient descent in the Edge of Stability regime, where the learning rate is large enough to induce persistent oscillations in the loss and the sharpness. We propose a continuous-time effective model that tracks the evolution of the average trajectory coupled with the time-averaged covariance of its fast oscillations. Our analysis reveals that the natural quantity to monitor in such unstable regimes is an effective free energy, which combines the original risk functional with a curvature-related "entropic" term. Our model allows us to track the envelope of the oscillations even in situations where its dynamics evolve on similar timescales as the averaged weights. Otherwise stated, we can track the spikes that occur during the training of some neural network architectures. For wide two-layer neural networks optimized under stable non-vanishing oscillations, we derive a mean-field limit that results in a novel kinetic equation describing the joint distribution of weights and their fluctuations. We show that this equation can be interpreted as a Wasserstein-2 gradient flow of a macroscopic free energy. Finally, we provide numerical evidence on matrix factorization and deep learning tasks (CIFAR-10) to demonstrate the model's accuracy in capturing the envelope of the oscillations and the predictive power of the effective free energy.
tldr: This paper studies gradient descent dynamics in the Edge of Stability regime using a free energy model and kinetic description for two-layer neural networks.
motivation: To understand the persistent oscillations in loss and sharpness observed when training neural networks with large learning rates.
method: Proposes a continuous-time effective model tracking average trajectory and time-averaged covariance, and derives a mean-field limit leading to a kinetic equation for wide two-layer networks.
result: Identifies an effective free energy combining risk and curvature-related entropy, and shows the kinetic equation is a Wasserstein-2 gradient flow of this free energy.
conclusion: The model accurately captures oscillation envelopes and the free energy predicts training dynamics, with numerical evidence on matrix factorization and CIFAR-10.

title: Automated Proving Of Shannon-Type Entropy Inequalities Via Fine-Tuned Language Models And Guided Tree Search
authors: Shing Yin Wong, Shaocheng Liu, Linqi Song, Amin Gohari, Cheuk Ting Li
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05729v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Proving Shannon-type entropy inequalities is a fundamental task in information theory that often requires constructing non-trivial linear combinations of known constraints, which is a combinatorial search problem that scales poorly with the number of random variables. We investigate whether small-scale large language models (0.6B--1.7B parameters), fine-tuned on atomic proof steps and combined with guided beam search, can automate this process. On a held-out test set of 60 inequalities spanning n=10 to 15 variables, our 0.6B fine-tuned model achieves an 85\% proof success rate with tree search. GPT-5.5 solves 1.7\% samples under zero-shot prompting while Psitip solves 33.3\% samples. A systematic ablation study across training context length (4096 vs.\ 8192 tokens) and data distribution (n=9-skewed vs not skewed) reveals that a 4096-token not skewed training distribution yields the best performance, with extended context and skewed data providing no marginal benefit. We further identify two dominant failure modes -- format failures and step quality degradation -- and verify that the beam-scoring heuristic is essential via a controlled ablation (random scoring reduces success from 83\% to 23\%).
tldr: This paper uses fine-tuned language models and guided tree search to automate the proving of Shannon-type entropy inequalities, achieving 85% success on a test set of 60 inequalities.
motivation: Proving Shannon-type entropy inequalities is a combinatorial search problem that scales poorly with the number of random variables, and existing automated tools have limited success.
method: Small-scale language models (0.6B–1.7B parameters) were fine-tuned on atomic proof steps and combined with guided beam search to generate proofs for entropy inequalities.
result: The 0.6B model achieved 85% proof success rate with tree search, outperforming GPT-5.5 (1.7%) and Psitip (33.3%). Ablation studies showed that 4096-token context and non-skewed training data were optimal.
conclusion: Fine-tuned language models with guided search can automate entropy inequality proving, but format failures and step quality degradation remain challenges; the beam-scoring heuristic is critical.

title: Compositional Boundaries For Density Fusion
authors: Ratan Bahadur Thapa, Ali Darijani, J\"urgen Beyerer, Steffen Staab
abstract: ArXiv:2606.05871v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Distributed uncertainty-management systems often combine local probabilistic models along aggregation trees chosen by communication, privacy, or scheduling constraints. The final density should depend on the weighted sources, not on the particular order in which intermediate nodes combine them. We study this requirement as an algebraic compositionality problem for binary fusion of weighted probability densities. The central question is when a local fusion rule can be executed hierarchically while remaining order-invariant. We establish a compositional boundary for local segment-valued fusion rules. Within the class of continuous binary rules with additive output weights and weight-only coefficients, order-invariant hierarchical execution characterizes normalized weighted linear pooling; norm-induced segment balancing realizes the corresponding coefficient. Smooth endpoint-to-candidate [MATH]-divergence balancing has a different local geometry: its quadratic expansion induces square-root effective weights, showing why pairwise solvability alone is insufficient for schedule-independent fusion. We show that this obstruction is local to endpoint-to-candidate binary balancing, whereas global divergence barycenters retain additive-weight local limits. Finally, Gaussian mixtures show how the same issue appears in finite model classes: exact fusion is compositional, whereas stepwise compression is compositional only under a congruence condition on unnormalized component measures. These results distinguish exact schedule-independent fusion from global aggregation objectives and local approximation heuristics.
tldr: This paper studies order-invariant hierarchical fusion of weighted probability densities, establishing that normalized weighted linear pooling is the only continuous binary rule with additive output weights that achieves compositional invariance.
motivation: Distributed uncertainty-management systems combine local probabilistic models along aggregation trees, and the final density should be independent of the order of combination. The paper aims to characterize when local fusion rules can be executed hierarchically while remaining order-invariant.
method: The authors formulate the problem as an algebraic compositionality problem for binary fusion of weighted probability densities. They analyze continuous binary rules with additive output weights and weight-only coefficients, and study local geometry of divergence balancing.
result: Order-invariant hierarchical execution characterizes normalized weighted linear pooling; norm-induced segment balancing realizes the corresponding coefficient. Smooth endpoint-to-candidate divergence balancing has a different local geometry that prevents schedule-independent fusion, whereas global divergence barycenters retain additive-weight local limits.
conclusion: The results distinguish exact schedule-independent fusion from global aggregation objectives and local approximation heuristics, highlighting that pairwise solvability is insufficient for schedule-independent fusion.

title: Swimming Against A Superfluid Flow: Self-Propulsion Via Vortex-Antivortex Shedding In A Quantum Fluid Of Light

We propose a fast and general predecision scheme for Metropolis Monte Carlo simulation of [MATH]-dimensional long-range interacting lattice models with [MATH] constituents. For potentials of the form [MATH], this reduces the computational complexity from [MATH] to [MATH] for $σ&…

result: They demonstrate that the system can host topological states and gauge-invariant dynamics, with potential for simulating lattice gauge theories.
conclusion: The work opens avenues for quantum simulation of topological gauge theories using cold atoms, but does not directly address information thermodynamics, quantum foundations, communication, or hybrid quantum systems.

authors: Ryosuke Yoshii And Rio Oto

tldr: This paper studies Kondo screening of topological bound states in an interacting Su-Schrieffer-Heeger chain, focusing on the control of the Kondo scale by topological mass.
motivation: To explore correlation effects beyond single-particle physics in topological systems, specifically how local Coulomb interactions at a domain wall soliton coupled to a metallic substrate give rise to Kondo screening.
method: The authors use theoretical modeling of an interacting Su-Schrieffer-Heeger chain with a domain wall, coupled to a metallic substrate, and analyze the Kondo effect via renormalization group or similar techniques.
result: They demonstrate that the Kondo temperature can be controlled by the topological mass (dimerization parameter), showing a non-trivial dependence.
conclusion: The work provides a platform for engineering Kondo physics in topological systems, with potential implications for quantum devices, but is not directly aligned with the user's research interests.

motivation: To understand how the Kondo effect is modified by strong correlations in one-dimensional fermionic environments, which are not captured by standard Fermi liquid theory.
method: The authors use theoretical methods such as bosonization and renormalization group analysis to study the quantum wire-impurity system.
result: They find that the Kondo singlet formation is suppressed or altered due to the repulsive nature of the impurity and the one-dimensional environment, leading to novel phases.
conclusion: The work provides a pathway to observe Kondo physics in cold atom systems, but the direct relevance to the user's interests in information thermodynamics, quantum foundations, communication, or hybrid quantum systems is limited.

result: The architecture achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on frustrated spin systems and quantum dynamics benchmarks.
conclusion: The work demonstrates the power of symmetry-aware transformers for quantum many-body problems, opening new avenues for neural quantum states.

title: Imaginary Time Spectral Transforms For Excited-state Preparation

result: Demonstrated on disordered spin chains, showing effective preparation of excited eigenstates.
conclusion: Provides a scalable approach for excited-state preparation, with potential applications in quantum simulation and hybrid algorithms.

authors: Itay Gomelski, Jonathan Elyovich, Ariel Kelman, Erez Zohar, And Patrick Emonts

[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023240] Published Tue Jun 02, 2026.
tldr: This paper develops algorithmic techniques for gauge fixing and enforcing translation invariance in gauged Gaussian fermionic projected entangled pair states (PEPS), advancing tensor network methods for lattice gauge theories.
motivation: Lattice gauge theories are crucial for nonperturbative physics but suffer from sign problems in Monte Carlo; tensor networks offer an alternative, but handling gauge symmetry and translation invariance algorithmically is challenging.
method: The authors propose algorithms for gauge fixing in Gaussian fermionic PEPS and for imposing translation invariance, leveraging the structure of Gaussian states and PEPS to reduce computational cost.
result: They demonstrate that gauge fixing can be performed efficiently and that translation invariance can be enforced without loss of accuracy, enabling simulation of larger systems.
conclusion: These algorithmic advances make tensor network simulations of lattice gauge theories more practical, potentially enabling studies of real-time dynamics and finite density.

tldr: This paper studies the interplay of twist and strain in bilayer graphene to engineer moiré patterns and narrow bands for correlated and topological phases.
motivation: To understand how strain, in addition to twist, can be used as a control knob for band engineering in bilayer graphene, potentially enabling new correlated and topological phases.
method: Theoretical modeling and simulations of strained and twisted bilayer graphene, likely using continuum models or tight-binding approaches.
result: Strain and twist together create moiré patterns and narrow bands that can host correlated and topological phases.
conclusion: Strain provides an additional realistic control for band engineering in bilayer graphene, complementing twist, with implications for quantum materials.

title: Evolving Disorder In non-Hermitian Lattices
authors: I. Komis, E. T. Kokkinakis, K. G. Makris, And E. N. Economou
abstract:

The impact of disorder on wave transport has been extensively studied in Hermitian systems, where static randomness gives rise to Anderson localization. [Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023227] Published Fri May 29, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies the effects of evolving disorder on wave transport in non-Hermitian lattices, revealing novel transport features distinct from static disorder.
motivation: While static disorder in non-Hermitian systems is known to cause jumpy wave evolution, the impact of time-varying (evolving) disorder remains unexplored.
method: The authors theoretically analyze wave propagation in non-Hermitian lattices with disorder that changes over time, using analytical and numerical methods.
result: Evolving disorder leads to unique transport phenomena not seen in static disorder, such as enhanced or suppressed localization depending on the evolution rate.
conclusion: The findings open new avenues for controlling wave transport in non-Hermitian systems, with potential applications in photonics and acoustics.

title: Spinor Pairing Order Enforced By Berry Phase
authors: Yi Li And Grayson R. Frazier
abstract:

Pairing between Fermi surfaces with unequal Chern-number parity is shown to produce an exotic superconducting state characterized by half-integer monopole harmonics and a spinor-valued order parameter. tldr: This paper predicts a novel superconducting state with spinor order parameter and half-integer monopole harmonics arising from pairing between Fermi surfaces of unequal Chern-number parity.
motivation: To explore exotic superconducting phases that emerge from topological band structures, specifically pairing between bands with different Chern numbers.
method: Theoretical analysis using topological band theory and Berry phase concepts to construct the pairing order parameter and derive its consequences.
result: Discovery of a spinor pairing order enforced by Berry phase, leading to a single Bogoliubov-Weyl node violating the Nielsen-Ninomiya theorem, protected gapless surface states, and a fractional Mermin-Ho relation.
conclusion: This work reveals a new class of topological superconductivity with potential implications for fault-tolerant quantum computing and topological quantum matter.

title: Taxonomy Of Prediction
authors: Alexandra Jurgens And James P. Crutchfield
abstract:

A prediction makes a claim about a system's future given knowledge of its past. A retrodiction makes a claim about its past given knowledge of its future. The bidirectional machine is an ambidextrous hidden Markov chain that does both optimally by making explicit in its state structure all statistic…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023218] Published Thu May 28, 2026.
tldr: The paper introduces the bidirectional machine, a hidden Markov model that optimally performs both prediction and retrodiction by encoding all statistical dependencies in its state structure.
motivation: To develop a unified framework for optimal prediction and retrodiction in stochastic processes, addressing the asymmetry between forward and backward inference.
method: The authors construct a bidirectional hidden Markov chain that captures both predictive and retrodictive statistics, leveraging computational mechanics and information theory.
result: The bidirectional machine achieves optimal prediction and retrodiction simultaneously, with state structure reflecting all relevant statistical dependencies.
conclusion: This work provides a theoretical foundation for ambidextrous inference, with potential applications in time series analysis and complex systems, but does not directly address quantum or thermodynamic aspects.

title: Symmetry And Self-bound Droplets In Dipolar Molecular Gases
authors: D. Baillie
abstract:
Author(s): D. Baillie

Recent experiments with degenerate molecular gases dressed by elliptically polarized microwave fields have enabled new control of dipolar interactions via engineered anisotropy. We reveal a symmetry structure of the dipolar interaction that generates degeneracies among the interaction parameters, en…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023219] Published Thu May 28, 2026.
tldr: This paper reveals a symmetry structure in dipolar interactions of molecular gases that leads to degeneracies among interaction parameters and enables self-bound droplets.
motivation: To understand the role of engineered anisotropy in dipolar molecular gases and to explore new quantum phases such as self-bound droplets.
method: Theoretical analysis of the dipolar interaction symmetry under elliptically polarized microwave dressing, combined with mean-field and beyond-mean-field calculations.
result: Discovery of a symmetry that creates degeneracies in interaction parameters, allowing for the formation of self-bound droplets in dipolar molecular gases.
conclusion: The findings provide a new control knob for quantum simulation and may lead to novel many-body states, but the direct connection to the user's research interests is weak.

method: The authors use theoretical modeling and simulations of electron transport in a two-terminal single-molecule junction setup, likely employing many-body techniques such as density functional theory or dynamical mean-field theory.
result: The paper demonstrates that organic open-shell molecules can host strongly correlated phenomena, influencing transport properties.
conclusion: The findings suggest that organic molecules are viable platforms for studying strongly correlated physics, with potential implications for molecular electronics and quantum materials.

motivation: To extend pulse-shaping capabilities from optical fields to freely propagating electrons, enabling coherent control of ultrafast quantum phenomena.

result: The paper demonstrates the feasibility of shaping electron pulses with femtosecond precision, analogous to optical pulse shapers.
conclusion: The work opens new possibilities for coherent control of electron beams, with potential applications in ultrafast electron microscopy and quantum optics, but is not directly relevant to the specified research directions.

conclusion: Provides a pathway for on-demand nonreciprocal devices in quantum networks, though not directly tied to the user's core interests.

Topological phenomena in quantum critical systems have recently attracted growing attention, as they go beyond the traditional paradigms of condensed matter and statistical physics. However, a general framework for identifying such nontrivial phenomena, particularly in higher-dimensional systems, re…

tldr: This paper generalizes the Li-Haldane correspondence to critical free-fermion systems, revealing topological features in quantum critical phases.
motivation: To extend the Li-Haldane correspondence, originally for 1D systems, to higher-dimensional critical free-fermion models, providing a general framework for identifying topological phenomena at quantum critical points.
method: Analytical and numerical study of entanglement spectra and topological invariants in free-fermion systems at criticality, using conformal field theory and lattice models.
result: Established a generalized correspondence between the entanglement spectrum and the edge state spectrum for critical free-fermion systems in arbitrary dimensions, showing that topological features persist at criticality.
conclusion: Provides a unified understanding of topological critical phenomena and opens avenues for exploring topological order in quantum critical systems beyond the traditional gapped phases.

method: Time-dependent density functional theory simulations of fermionic superfluid rings with varying impurity density and size in the BCS regime.
result: The critical winding number for vortex emission increases with impurity density, indicating impurity-controlled dissipation.
conclusion: Impurities can enhance stability of persistent currents, offering a mechanism to control dissipation in superfluid systems.

motivation: Ollivier-Ricci curvature is useful for analyzing network structures, but classical computation is expensive; a quantum algorithm could offer speedup.
method: The authors design a quantum algorithm that leverages amplitude estimation and quantum walks to estimate the curvature, likely with a quadratic speedup over classical methods.
result: The algorithm provides a quantum speedup for computing Ollivier-Ricci curvature, though the exact complexity and practical advantages depend on graph properties.

method: Theoretical analysis using topological criticality and anyon condensation concepts.
result: Topological criticality enables anyonic exciton superfluids with non-Abelian statistics.

result: The ground state exhibits hidden time-reversal symmetry breaking, and the transition belongs to the three-dimensional XY universality class.
conclusion: The findings provide insight into frustrated magnetism and may guide studies of topological phases in kagome systems.

result: A complete stochastic calculus for pathwise observables of Markov-jump processes, unifying diffusion and jump dynamics.

conclusion: The findings highlight the role of radiative loss in stealthy hyperuniform systems and may impact the design of photonic devices.

title: 2d Van Der Waals Magnets: From Fundamental Physics To Applications
authors: Je-Geun Park, Kai-Xuan Zhang, Hyeonsik Cheong, Jae Hoon Kim, Carina A. Belvin, David Hsieh, Honglie Ning, And Nuh Gedik
abstract:
Author(s): Je-Geun Park, Kai-Xuan Zhang, Hyeonsik Cheong, Jae Hoon Kim, Carina A. Belvin, David Hsieh, Honglie Ning, and Nuh Gedik

Scientific discovery is often described as walking into a dark room and turning on the light. The discovery of 2D magnetism in van der Waals materials in 2016 was one such leap forward, removing one spatial dimension from macroscopic materials. The study of 2D magnets has challenged established theories and uncovered new phenomena. This review summarizes the current state of knowledge of magnetic phenomena in 2D van der Waals materials. The field encompasses not just the traditional study of ferromagnets and antiferromagnets but also topology, quantum and nonequilibrium dynamics, Floquet effects, magnons and spintronics, and the interaction of magnetism with light, phonons, and electric fields (multiferroics). The field is actively evolving, expanding theoretical understanding, materials capabilities, and experimental phenomenology while opening new directions for application.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025003] Published Wed May 27, 2026.
tldr: A review of 2D van der Waals magnets covering fundamental physics and applications.
motivation: To summarize the current state of knowledge and recent discoveries in 2D magnetism since its experimental realization in 2016.
method: Review article summarizing experimental and theoretical progress in 2D van der Waals magnetic materials.
result: The field encompasses ferromagnets, antiferromagnets, topology, quantum dynamics, Floquet effects, magnons, spintronics, and multiferroics.
conclusion: The field is actively evolving, expanding theoretical understanding and experimental capabilities, with potential applications.

Applications discussed include trapping and manipulation of atoms and nanoparticles by light, sorting of biological cells by the combination of acoustics and microfluidics, and pulling forces that draw particles against the direction of wave propagation.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025002] Published Thu Apr 30, 2026.

motivation: To provide a comprehensive and unified perspective on how wave fields exert forces and torques on particles, a topic with applications in trapping, manipulation, and sorting.
method: The authors review theoretical frameworks and experimental results, emphasizing the role of local densities of energy, momentum, and spin in both optical and acoustic contexts.
result: They show that forces and torques can be understood from the same underlying principles in optics and acoustics, and discuss applications such as optical tweezers, acoustic sorting, and pulling forces.
conclusion: The unified framework aids in designing advanced particle manipulation techniques and may inspire cross-disciplinary innovations.

title: Exactly Solvable Quantum Many-body Dynamics From Space-time Duality
authors: Bruno Bertini, Pieter W. Claeys, And Tomaž Prosen
abstract:
Author(s): Bruno Bertini, Pieter W. Claeys, and Tomaž Prosen

Computing quantum dynamics in many-body systems is notoriously difficult. In the past decade, there has been a fundamental advance based on discretizing the time evolution of lattice systems, by analogy with digital computation. Since space is already discrete on a lattice, treating space and time on the same footing avoids the mathematical complications of continuous space-time quantum field theories. This review focuses on how this space-time duality plays out in the dynamics of interacting many-body systems and the intrinsic relationship with special kinds of lattices termed brickwork quantum circuits. From this pedagogical review, readers will learn how this far-reaching analogy with quantum computation lies at the heart of a unified view of dynamical evolution of quantum many-body systems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025001] Published Wed Apr 15, 2026.
tldr: This review discusses space-time duality in quantum many-body dynamics using brickwork quantum circuits, focusing on exactly solvable models.
motivation: To provide a pedagogical overview of how space-time duality and brickwork circuits enable exact solutions for quantum many-body dynamics.
method: Review of theoretical framework based on space-time duality and brickwork quantum circuits, with examples of exactly solvable models.
result: Unified view of dynamical evolution in quantum many-body systems via analogy with quantum computation.
conclusion: Space-time duality offers a powerful tool for understanding quantum dynamics, with potential for further developments in integrable and non-integrable systems.

title: Kagome Metals
authors: Domenico Di Sante, Titus Neupert, Giorgio Sangiovanni, Ronny Thomale, Riccardo Comin, Joseph G. Checkelsky, Ilija Zeljkovic, And Stephen D. Wilson
abstract:
Author(s): Domenico Di Sante, Titus Neupert, Giorgio Sangiovanni, Ronny Thomale, Riccardo Comin, Joseph G. Checkelsky, Ilija Zeljkovic, and Stephen D. Wilson

The kagome lattice is a two-dimensional tiling of hexagons and triangles named after a Japanese basket weaving technique. Its geometry gives rise to highly frustrated interactions and interference effects experienced by electrons and their multiple degrees of freedom. In metals, the exploration of materials with kagome conduction networks is driven by predictions of realizing new electronic states where these interference effects are dominant, amplifying electronic interactions and many-body effects. In these kagome metals, these amplified correlation effects in combination with spin-orbit coupling and other forms of frustration have given rise to a wealth of phenomena beyond expectations. These include unusual states and responses born from topological flat bands, massive Dirac fermions, sublattice interference effects at saddle points such as unconventional superconductivity, orbital antiferromagnetism and flux phases, amplified anomalous Hall effects, and electronic nematic states. This review examines the theoretical and experimental work on kagome metals, with the aim of elucidating fundamental mechanisms underlying the observed exotic phenomena.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 015002] Published Thu Feb 12, 2026.
tldr: A review of kagome metals, focusing on exotic electronic states arising from frustrated lattice geometry.
motivation: To understand the fundamental mechanisms behind unusual phenomena in kagome metals, such as unconventional superconductivity and topological flat bands.
method: Review of theoretical and experimental work on kagome metals, summarizing key findings and open questions.
result: Kagome metals exhibit a wealth of exotic states including topological flat bands, massive Dirac fermions, unconventional superconductivity, orbital antiferromagnetism, and electronic nematicity.
conclusion: The review elucidates the role of frustration and interference effects in kagome metals, providing a foundation for future research on correlated topological materials.

title: Field Theories And Quantum Methods For Stochastic Reaction-diffusion Systems
authors: Mauricio J. Del Razo, Tommaso Lamma, And Wout Merbis
abstract:
Author(s): Mauricio J. del Razo, Tommaso Lamma, and Wout Merbis

The exchange of energy and molecules in a living cell, the spread of opinions through a society, and the flow of traffic in a crowded city are very different phenomena, yet they are all examples of complex systems composed of many agents that interact with each other and exchange energy or particles with the environment. These systems can be modeled as stochastic reaction-diffusion systems. In this pedagogical review, the authors apply powerful field-theoretic methods to these systems, unifying diverse approaches under a single framework. The methods are useful for handling chemical systems but also have applications in a wide range of areas such as ecology and epidemiology.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 015001] Published Thu Jan 22, 2026.
tldr: This pedagogical review applies field-theoretic methods to stochastic reaction-diffusion systems, unifying diverse approaches for modeling complex systems in chemistry, ecology, and epidemiology.
motivation: To provide a unified framework for stochastic reaction-diffusion systems using field-theoretic methods, which are powerful but often scattered across different disciplines.
method: The authors review and apply field-theoretic techniques, such as path integrals and Doi-Peliti formalism, to stochastic reaction-diffusion equations.
result: They demonstrate how these methods can handle chemical systems and extend to applications in ecology and epidemiology, offering a coherent perspective.
conclusion: The review serves as a pedagogical resource, potentially inspiring further cross-disciplinary applications of field theory in stochastic systems.

authors: E. D. Dahlberg, I. González-Adalid Pemartín, E. Marinari, G. Parisi, F. Ricci-Tersenghi, V. Martin-Mayor, J. Moreno-Gordo, R. L. Orbach, I. Paga, J. J. Ruiz-Lorenzo, And D. Yllanes
abstract:
Author(s): E. D. Dahlberg, I. González-Adalid Pemartín, E. Marinari, G. Parisi, F. Ricci-Tersenghi, V. Martin-Mayor, J. Moreno-Gordo, R. L. Orbach, I. Paga, J. J. Ruiz-Lorenzo, and D. Yllanes

This review updates the field of spin glasses with broad application to a large variety of physical systems. In particular, this review tracks the progress of experiment, theory, and large-scale simulations. It highlights the importance of their synergy, from the inception of the field to the present day, and includes future opportunities for research.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045005] Published Mon Dec 15, 2025.
tldr: A review of spin-glass dynamics covering experiment, theory, and simulation, with emphasis on their synergy.
motivation: To update the field of spin glasses, which has broad applications to many physical systems, and to highlight progress and future opportunities.
method: Review of experimental, theoretical, and large-scale simulation studies, synthesizing results from the inception of the field to the present.
result: The review tracks progress in understanding spin-glass dynamics and emphasizes the importance of combining experiment, theory, and simulation.
conclusion: The field continues to offer opportunities for research, particularly through the synergy of different approaches.

title: Kitaev Quantum Spin Liquids
authors: Yuji Matsuda, Takasada Shibauchi, And Hae-Young Kee
abstract:
Author(s): Yuji Matsuda, Takasada Shibauchi, and Hae-Young Kee

Frustration in spin systems can prevent ordering even at =0, creating quantum spin liquids that have been sought since Anderson’s pioneering work in 1973 and his influential 1987 paper connecting them to high-temperature superconductivity. Kitaev’s solvable spin-1/2 models on a honeycomb lattice brought renewed attention to this field, with Jackeli and Khaliullin later revealing how to engineer Kitaev interactions in real materials. This review highlights theoretical and experimental developments in Kitaev spin liquids, emphasizing leading candidate materials and their broad topological properties such as chiral edge modes. Consequently, it provides essential insights for both experimentalists and theorists working on quantum spin liquid problems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045003] Published Wed Dec 03, 2025.
tldr: This review covers theoretical and experimental progress in Kitaev quantum spin liquids, focusing on candidate materials and topological properties.
motivation: To provide a comprehensive overview of Kitaev spin liquids, which are a major topic in condensed matter physics but not directly related to the user's interests in information thermodynamics, quantum foundations, quantum communication, or hybrid quantum systems.
method: Review of theoretical models (Kitaev honeycomb model) and experimental realizations in materials like α-RuCl3, summarizing key results and open questions.
result: Highlights chiral edge modes and other topological features, and discusses leading candidate materials.
conclusion: The paper is essential for condensed matter physicists studying spin liquids but has minimal overlap with the user's specified research directions.

title: The Ups And Downs Of Internal Conversion
authors: Anjay Manian, Zifei Chen, Hugh T. Sullivan, And Salvy P. Russo
abstract:
Author(s): Anjay Manian, Zifei Chen, Hugh T. Sullivan, and Salvy P. Russo

This review examines the theoretical methods used to describe the photophysical process of internal conversion in quantum systems. These models explore all facets of the nonradiative mechanism, and the review presents an outlook on how they can be incorporated in studies relevant to applications, for example, in photonics and energy harvesting.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 035003] Published Tue Sep 16, 2025.
tldr: This review covers theoretical methods for internal conversion in quantum systems, focusing on nonradiative transitions and their applications in photonics and energy harvesting.
motivation: To provide a comprehensive overview of theoretical models describing internal conversion, a key photophysical process, and to highlight how these models can be applied in practical fields like photonics and energy harvesting.
method: The paper is a review that surveys various theoretical approaches, likely including quantum dynamics, rate theories, and computational methods, to model internal conversion.
result: The review summarizes the current state of theoretical methods for internal conversion and discusses their integration into application-oriented studies.
conclusion: The authors suggest that improved theoretical models of internal conversion can enhance the design of photonic and energy-harvesting devices, but the paper does not present new findings or direct connections to the user's specific research interests.

title: Photoinduced Nonequilibrium States In Mott Insulators
authors: Yuta Murakami, Denis Golež, Martin Eckstein, And Philipp Werner
abstract:
Author(s): Yuta Murakami, Denis Golež, Martin Eckstein, and Philipp Werner

The interplay between nonequilibrium physics and strong electronic correlations offers a unique platform for manipulating material properties, exploring novel optical responses, and uncovering quantum metastable phases. This review provides a comprehensive overview of recent advances in understanding the nonequilibrium dynamics of photoexcited Mott insulators—systems where strong interactions and a robust energy gap can give rise to rich and controllable phenomena. We discuss various nonlinear and nonperturbative pathways for driving and controlling Mott insulators using strong static or periodic fields. Furthermore, the review highlights key mechanisms that govern the evolution of photodoped carriers and the emergence of metastable and nonthermal states characterized by superconducting, magnetic, orbital, and excitonic orders.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 035001] Published Thu Jul 31, 2025.
tldr: A review of nonequilibrium dynamics in photoexcited Mott insulators, focusing on strong correlations and photoinduced phase transitions.
motivation: To understand and control material properties using light in strongly correlated systems, particularly Mott insulators.
method: Comprehensive review of theoretical and experimental advances, discussing nonlinear and nonperturbative driving mechanisms.
result: Key mechanisms for photodoped carrier evolution and emergence of metastable phases with superconducting, magnetic, orbital, and excitonic orders.
conclusion: Provides a framework for future research on light-induced control of quantum materials, but does not directly address information thermodynamics, quantum foundations, communication, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Colloquium: Quantum Properties And Functionalities Of Magnetic Skyrmions
authors: Alexander P. Petrović, Christina Psaroudaki, Peter Fischer, Markus Garst, And Christos Panagopoulos
abstract:
Author(s): Alexander P. Petrović, Christina Psaroudaki, Peter Fischer, Markus Garst, and Christos Panagopoulos

Skyrmions are topological field configurations that were first discussed in the context of high-energy theory. In recent years, skyrmionic spin patterns in solid-state systems have received much attention, in part for their promising application potential. This Colloquium discusses quantum-mechanical aspects of such magnetic skyrmions, both for the interactions that underlie skyrmion formation and for quantum features of the skyrmions themselves.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 031001] Published Tue Jul 08, 2025.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews quantum-mechanical aspects of magnetic skyrmions, including their formation interactions and quantum features.
motivation: To provide a comprehensive overview of quantum properties of magnetic skyrmions, which have been studied mainly classically, and to highlight their potential for quantum technologies.
method: Review of theoretical and experimental literature on quantum aspects of skyrmions, covering interactions underlying skyrmion formation and quantum features of skyrmions themselves.
result: The paper discusses quantum effects in skyrmion dynamics, quantum tunneling, and entanglement, but does not present new results.
conclusion: Quantum skyrmions may offer new functionalities for quantum information processing, but the field is still nascent.

title: Spin-dependent Exotic Interactions
authors: Lei Cong, Wei Ji, Pavel Fadeev, Filip Ficek, Min Jiang, Victor V. Flambaum, Haosen Guan, Derek F. Jackson Kimball, Mikhail G. Kozlov, Yevgeny V. Stadnik, And Dmitry Budker
abstract:
Author(s): Lei Cong, Wei Ji, Pavel Fadeev, Filip Ficek, Min Jiang, Victor V. Flambaum, Haosen Guan, Derek F. Jackson Kimball, Mikhail G. Kozlov, Yevgeny V. Stadnik, and Dmitry Budker

This review presents a comprehensive summary of theoretical investigations and experimental searches for spin-dependent interactions beyond the standard model. These interactions may be mediated by various types of exotic bosons, and their existence and properties may, in turn, explain the nature of dark matter and dark energy. The described experiments also probe the discrete fundamental symmetries of nature.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025005] Published Tue Jun 24, 2025.
tldr: A comprehensive review of theoretical and experimental searches for spin-dependent exotic interactions beyond the Standard Model, including their possible role in dark matter and dark energy.
motivation: To systematically survey the landscape of spin-dependent forces mediated by exotic bosons, which could reveal new physics beyond the Standard Model and shed light on dark matter and dark energy.
method: The paper is a review that summarizes theoretical frameworks (e.g., effective field theories) and experimental techniques (e.g., precision magnetometry, atomic spectroscopy) used to probe spin-dependent interactions.
result: The review catalogs numerous experimental constraints on spin-dependent couplings and discusses the potential of future experiments to discover new bosons or test discrete symmetries.
conclusion: Spin-dependent exotic interactions remain a promising avenue for discovering new physics, and ongoing experimental improvements will continue to tighten constraints or potentially yield discoveries.

title: Colloquium: Qudits For Decomposing Multiqubit Gates And Realizing Quantum Algorithms
authors: Evgeniy O. Kiktenko, Anastasiia S. Nikolaeva, And Aleksey K. Fedorov
abstract:
Author(s): Evgeniy O. Kiktenko, Anastasiia S. Nikolaeva, and Aleksey K. Fedorov

Two-level systems—bits or qubits—are understood to generally be the most efficient primitives for information processing, classical or quantum. But this is not to say that there are no roles to be played by multilevel systems. This Colloquium surveys these possible roles for the quantum case. Here we speak of qudits:
[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 021003] Published Tue Jun 03, 2025.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews the use of qudits (multilevel quantum systems) for decomposing multiqubit gates and implementing quantum algorithms, highlighting potential simplifications like the Toffoli gate using qutrits.
motivation: To survey the roles of qudits in quantum computing, challenging the assumption that qubits are always optimal, and to explore practical advantages in gate decomposition and algorithm realization.
method: The paper provides a review of qudit-qubit embeddings, theoretical frameworks for gate decomposition using qudits, and a survey of experimental implementations.
result: Qudits can simplify certain quantum gates (e.g., Toffoli gate with a qutrit) and may reduce resource requirements in quantum algorithms, though practical challenges remain.
conclusion: Qudits offer alternative approaches for quantum computing, but their advantages depend on the specific context; further experimental progress is needed to assess their viability.

title: Colloquium: Materials That Exceed Classical Thermodynamic Bounds On Properties
authors: Roderic S. Lakes
abstract:
Author(s): Roderic S. Lakes

Classical thermodynamic bounds provide constraints on values that are expected in measurements of certain physical properties. In a variety of fields, some measurements exceed these bounds. This apparent violation of thermodynamics arises because the measurements are made in ways that violate the underlying assumptions made when deriving these bounds. This Colloquium describes a wide variety of circumstances where such violations occur and which of the underlying assumptions are violated in each case. It also describes how interesting material properties can be developed using materials designed to violate these assumptions.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 021002] Published Wed May 14, 2025.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews materials that appear to exceed classical thermodynamic bounds on physical properties, explaining how violations arise from measurement conditions that break underlying assumptions.
motivation: To clarify why some measurements of material properties exceed classical thermodynamic bounds and to explore how materials can be designed to exploit these violations.
method: Review of a wide variety of circumstances where measured properties exceed thermodynamic bounds, analyzing which assumptions are violated in each case.
result: Many apparent violations are due to measurements made under conditions that violate assumptions such as equilibrium, linearity, or homogeneity; materials can be engineered to deliberately violate these assumptions to achieve enhanced properties.
conclusion: Understanding the assumptions behind thermodynamic bounds enables the design of materials with properties beyond classical limits, with implications for metamaterials and composite design.

title: Codata Recommended Values Of The Fundamental Physical Constants: 2022
authors: Peter J. Mohr, David B. Newell, Barry N. Taylor, And Eite Tiesinga
abstract:
Author(s): Peter J. Mohr, David B. Newell, Barry N. Taylor, and Eite Tiesinga

This review contains the 2022 self-consistent set of values of the constants and conversion factors of physics and chemistry recommended by the Committee on Data for Science and Technology (CODATA). The CODATA values are based on a least-squares adjustment that takes into account all data available up to the end of 2022. Details of the data selection and methodology are described.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025002] Published Wed Apr 30, 2025.
